utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-95-16-T, the Prosecutor versus Zoran Kupreskic, Mirjan Kupreskic, Vlatko Kupreskic, Drago Josipovic, Dragan Papic, Vladimir Santic, also known as "Vlado."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning. Before I ask the Prosecutor to call in their next witness, let me draw your attention to a motion filed on the 17th of September by the accused Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez for access to non-public materials in this case. I wonder whether the Prosecution or the Defence could give us their comments, their oral comments, say on Wednesday or Thursday before we decide? We would like to know what they think about this motion. Is it fine with you if we receive your comments on Wednesday morning? Yes. Wednesday morning? Yes. Good. So we can now proceed with the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Mr. President, with the permission of the Court, while we are waiting for the next witness, we filed today an order of witness appearance for this week, and we wish to draw attention to a slight change in order. Witness No. 2 on our present list will now appear in place of Witness No. 4. So, in effect, Witness No. 2 becomes Witness No. 4 and Witness No. 3 becomes Witness No. 2 and Witness No. 4 becomes Witness No. 3, if that's clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Since we are still waiting for the witness -- (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: -- I wonder whether you have submitted to the Trial Chamber the statement of Witness No. 11 because -- probably this is because of my messy file, but I can't find, in my file, his or her statement, but this may be my own problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Our records show that the statement was filed and presented to the Court, but it may be that there was some confusion about the name, and what we will do, that is, if, in fact, the Court is having difficulty finding it, we will simply submit another statement today, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. I understand we will use a pseudonym for the present witness. It will be Witness M. Witness M, may I ask you to stand up and read the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. The microphone isn't switched on. Microphone, please. I'm afraid we can't hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I'm afraid the interpreters can't hear the witness. I wonder whether you could put the microphone in front of the witness? Could you please repeat your declaration, because we could not hear the translation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: But we still can't hear the witness very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Mr. President, I am now requesting the usher to hand to the witness the Prosecutor's next exhibit, a piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: But I'm afraid we still can't hear the witness very well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document is marked Exhibit 178.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: May I ask the usher to make sure that the witness speaks into the microphone because the interpreters said that they still can't hear the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness M.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Radovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: I think that is her real name because the first is "ch," not "sh." You know our ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Can you show it to Counsel Radovic (referring to Exhibit 178)? Thank you, Counsel Radovic, for drawing our attention to a slight misprint or typo or whatever. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness M.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: (Interpretation inaudible)

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: I want to assure you that you have been granted by this Tribunal the protection measures that you have requested. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: (Interpretation inaudible)

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: So you may feel confident to provide full and clear testimony here today.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: (Interpretation inaudible)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: The answer was not translated. Can the interpreters hear the witness? Yes. You may proceed. I hope we no longer have any problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Witness M, could you tell us in what year you were born?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: (Interpretation inaudible)

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Witness M, we're having a little technical difficulty with the translation, so that is why there is this delay, so please bear with us.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: A moment ago, we couldn't hear anything. Whether we can hear now, I don't know, because the microphone isn't being used.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Witness M, I'm going to have to ask you what year you were born again, ask you that question again, and then we will see if the microphone is working. I know this is probably the wrong question to have to repeat, but it seems like the logical one. Could you tell us again what year you were born in, and speak into the microphone, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, without naming the members of your family, could you describe for us your family, the composition of your family, in 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: I had three sons, two daughters, three grandchildren, myself, and my husband.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Do you recall when you came to the village of Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Do you remember the year?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Where was your home village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: In Karaula.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Why didn't you stay in Karaula?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: We couldn't stay there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: What happened there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: Well, what happened was that we had to evacuate to Travnik because of the war. I don't know, really. They took us down there to Travnik. That's what had to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Did you remain in Travnik, or did you have to leave Travnik as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: We were in Travnik for some time, and when Karaula fell, we left to Vitez to Dubravica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: About how long did you spend in Dubravica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: Only three days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Where did you go after you left Dubravica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: To Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Do you remember the place that you went to in Ahmici, the house you went to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: I remember. Of course, I remember. It's as if I saw the house now, but it doesn't exist anymore. It's sort of disappeared.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Who is the owner of that house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: (redacted).

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Are you related to (redacted).

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: No. No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: How did it come that you went to his house to live when you came to Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: Through some friends of ours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Were you living (redacted), you and your family, living with (redacted) just before the attack began in 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: Yes. I know that the closest neighbour was Vlatko Kupreskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Did you know Vlatko Kupreskic by sight? Could you recognise him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: No. No. No, I couldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Do you know where he lived and what his house looked like?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: Yes, the house wasn't far off (redacted) house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Could you see Vlatko Kupreskic's house from (redacted)?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: Yes, we could see it from the house through the window. We had a constant view of Vlatko's house; and when the light was on downstairs, you could see people moving about, the mother probably. I don't know who the father was. But it's not far.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Just perhaps to orient us a little more, do you recall who some of your closest Muslim neighbours were in that neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. There was Redzib Ahmic, Meho Hrustanovic, Krdzalic Huso, Sakib Ahmic and his two sons, Naser, Sukrija, Budo. Behind (redacted), I don't know the surname of those -- that man.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, outside of (redacted), was there some sort of water spout or water tap, and if there was, could you tell us where it was outside or in relation to (redacted)?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: Yes, I can. The next house to Vlatko's, up above towards (redacted) on the right-hand side, the corner of the house, the first corner as you look at the house from the bottom, there was a water tap.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Did you occasionally use that water tap while you were living in (redacted)?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: Yes, all the time. That's where we did the washing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Could you see Vlatko's house from that water tap?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I could. Of course, I could. How could we not see it, because it was close? I don't know the exact distance, though. But, of course, Vlatko's house is very close to (redacted).

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, do you remember the day of the attack, and without describing what happened that day, my question is just: Do you remember that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, I want to draw your attention to the day or evening before the attack. Do you recall being at the water tap on that day, the day before the attack?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It was a Thursday, the 15th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: While you were at the water tap on the 15th of April, did you happen to look at Vlatko Kupreskic's house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps I would not have looked at it, but I heard a vehicle of some kind, and I looked up and saw that a truck had come with the army, with soldiers. I would not have known that they were soldiers had I not seen them getting out below Vlatko's house, the basement, below Vlatko's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, can you recall what kind of truck this was? Can you describe it in any way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: No, I can't. I have forgotten what kind of truck. I can't tell you that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned soldiers. Where did you see these soldiers coming from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: Well, they came from down there, down the Makadim road surface, on the road, and they came to the basement below Vlatko's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Did you see the soldiers go into Vlatko's house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: Not that. No, I didn't. The entrance to Vlatko's house is by the road, but they went below, in front of the basement, below his house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Is this the basement of Vlatko's house that you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: Well, there was a warehouse of some kind. What it was, I don't know. But that's where they were. It was something strange that he had down below, but it was like a basement, a sort of storage place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Do you recall how many soldiers you saw?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: No. No, I don't. I didn't count them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Could you give us an idea as to whether it was one or two or ten or more?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: I don't know. I can say perhaps five, five or six. I stopped looking. I went away. I washed my shoes at the water tap and I went back home.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that these people that you saw, that they were soldiers. How did you know they were soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: Well, how wouldn't I know that they were soldiers? I saw all the equipment that an army carries, both ours and theirs. I saw the uniforms, I saw that they were soldiers. I recognised them. That's what they were. Exactly that. They were equipped with uniforms, they were military in appearance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: At this time, I would ask the usher to show to the witness previously entered Exhibit 32, P32, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, Witness M, could you look at your TV screen and tell us if you recognise what is shown there, and this is previously admitted Exhibit 32. Can you tell us what that shows?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: Yes, I can. I can say quite freely that on the picture you can see Vlatko Kupreskic's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, does this --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Does this picture show --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: Mm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: -- where you saw the truck the day before the attack?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: No. It shows the entrance from the road into Vlatko's house. The road was down below, and that's Vlatko's house. I looked at that house for five months, just as I'm looking at it now. I passed by it several times, both down below and from the top part. I would return home using the top part.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Just to clarify something. You mentioned a basement a little while ago and that the soldiers went into a basement. Was the basement located in this house where you saw the soldiers go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: Below. Down below the house, and the house is up above, above this level.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And when you saw the soldiers go into the basement, did you see the soldiers before they went into the basement? Did you see them coming out of the truck or were they already out of the truck when you first saw them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: I saw them getting out, getting down from the truck. They probably couldn't -- could not have just disappeared into the ground. They entered somewhere down below. Whether it was a basement or a storage of some kind, a warehouse, that's where they went. They would go down towards that level.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, did you tell anyone what you had seen that day, tell your husband or anyone else that you had seen some soldiers coming out of a truck and entering --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Why --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: I didn't think of doing that. I didn't think why they had come, what they were doing there, why they were there. This was something that I didn't think about at all, and I didn't think that I -- I didn't say anything, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, I want to focus your attention to the morning of the next day, the day of April 16, 1993. Could you tell us what you remember of that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: Yes, I can. On that day, I remember in the morning of the 16th of April, it was a Friday, I was sleeping up in Redzib's weekend house with his daughter. She had two children. She was alone. I slept there at their place. In the morning, about twenty or twenty-five minutes to six, there was gunfire around the weekend cottage, on the window panes and the doors, and we left the -- we went out of that weekend cottage and went up towards Redzib's house. It was raining. We stopped there a little while. We couldn't stay, and we went towards the hill. We went up to Vrhovine. That is a village. We were told that we couldn't stay there either, because the village would be granaded. And we went further on, up to the village of Poculica. We came there. We spent ten days with a man there. On the eleventh day, they displaced us from there and sent us to a Croatian house. We spent only three days there, and then they moved us again to another Croatian house, and we stayed there until Slimena fell, near Travnik. Then from the command headquarters they gave us a car, a vehicle came to fetch us, and took us to Slimena, to a third Croatian house. We stayed there for two and a half years. When Karaula fell, when Karaula was liberated and when a Serb village named Varosluk fell up, up above Turbe, we went there to(redacted), and that was the seventh place we stayed at, our seventh homestead. And now we're nowhere actually, and we didn't go anywhere else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, Witness M, I would like to ask just a couple of questions to clarify some of that. You said that on the 16th of April, in Ahmici, you spent the evening before the attack sleeping at a weekend house. How close --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: Yes, just prior to the attack. I spent the time in this weekend cottage, Redzib's cottage.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: (redacted)?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: (redacted).

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, when you fled from Ahmici, from the weekend house, did you see any burning in the village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: Yes, I did, and anybody could have seen that who was alive to see it. Everybody could see that. We didn't move away from Redzib's house much, some 50 metres away, and the whole of the village was in flames. And we couldn't see anything else, just the fire, the flames, and we heard shooting, nothing else. And we just moved up, further up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Do you recall any particular houses you can identify that you saw on fire as you fled from Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: Yes, I remember the houses, but I don't know if I could recognise them now because they were alight. You know, when a house is on fire, the house is no longer -- no longer stands complete. I know all the houses, but once they're set afire to, I don't know. I don't know if I could recognise any of them now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And just one final question: Do you remember what time of day it was? And now I'm talking about the day before the attack when you saw the soldiers around Vlatko's house, about what time of day it was that you saw that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: It was in the evening hours. I didn't look at my watch. My daughter had come back home from work, she went to work that day in Slimena in Olip. I don't know what the time was, but it was just before about dusk, roundabout dusk. It was still daylight, but I don't know the exact time. I didn't look to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: May I have just a moment, Mr. President? We have no more questions for this witness, and request that Exhibit 178 be admitted under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: Thank you and good-bye.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: No, no. Witness M, you must remain here, and I will turn to Counsel Pavkovic to ask --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: -- which counsel are going to cross-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I should like to inform you that the Counsel Krajina, Ranko Radovic and, I believe, Ms. Slokovic-Glumac, will be interrogating the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Counsel Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Please, Madam, I just have one question to ask of you. You said that you lived at the house of (redacted)?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Did you, on the 15th of April, 1993, see (redacted)?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: No, I didn't see that man at all. Whether he'd gone somewhere I don't know, but he wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Who was with you in the house, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: On that particular day, who was with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: (redacted) was with me, my daughter, my son was there, who had had an operation. He had his appendix out and he was at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Very well. Did (redacted) come to your house at all that day -- go home that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: I don't know. I just don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: You don't know? Did you see him at all that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Of course, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Where did you see him? A.(redacted) was at home, but at that particular time, during the time that I was at the water tap, I don't know. He spent the night in his house, and in the morning they fled as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: No, I'm asking you about the day before the attack, on the 15th of April.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: On Thursday you mean. Yes, he was at home. (redacted) was at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: He was at home?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Did he go any somewhere, leave his home at all that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't say. I can't tell you what I didn't see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Just a moment. Did you spend the whole day at home?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: Were you at home the whole day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Where did you go when you were not at home?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: I wasn't at home the whole day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Well, where were you that day? Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: We went visiting to upper Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: When did you go visiting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: Well, in the morning, about lunch time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Who went with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: (redacted) wife, I, myself, (redacted) (redacted). We went up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: How long did you stay?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: Well, about two and a half hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Did you all come back together?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: Yes, we all came back together.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Where was (redacted) at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: I don't know. Probably went somewhere. I don't know where he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Was he in the house when you returned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: You don't know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: When you left for this visit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: You don't know that either?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: I didn't pay any attention to that, because I was in one room, they were in the other room.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Did you see him at all that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: Yes, I did see (redacted) the morning and would I see him every morning. I had to see him every morning because he had breakfast with us every morning and drank coffee with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Well, would he go out somewhere?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: Yes, he went out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: When would he return?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: Roundabout -- well, in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: In the evening you say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: Yes. (redacted) come back in the evening as it became dark. He would be working with the Croat neighbours, at the Croat neighbour's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Did you see him come back that particular day if he did come back from work that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: No, I didn't. Whether he went out anywhere to work that day I don't know. I just know that he was at home in the morning, and we went up to the village later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. President, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASESSE
utterances.text: Thank you, Counsel Krajina. Counsel Radovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you had three sons and a husband. I should like to know whether any of your sons had served the army or had joined the Territorial Defence Forces?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: All three of them were with the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So they were not with you in the house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: They would be in the house when they came from the so-called lines. They would come for a rest, for a night or two.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: But on the 15th of April, the day prior to the attack, were they with you or were they at the frontlines?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: Two were not with me, they were at the frontlines.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: And the third one?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: He had had an operation and was --

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Was he in the house on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me about the son who came from the front-line, and was he at the house on the eve of the attack. Did he have a uniform on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: Yes, he was wearing a uniform. He came wearing a uniform, which is normal in the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: And when you were fleeing from the house, was he fleeing wearing his uniform or in mufti?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: No, he was in his uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: And it was in the uniform that he was fleeing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: Yes. He went out of the house in the uniform. He was sick. He was due to appear before a medical board in three days and then after that to return to the front-line. He could not appear before that Commission, and the very third day he was returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. You didn't understand what I asked. On that morning when your son was fleeing, was he fleeing in a uniform or civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: He was in a uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: And to Vrhovine he went with you, in the uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Did he bring with him any weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: No, he had not brought any weapons. They never did that. They would leave the arms in Travnik, up there in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Why was that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Didn't they tell you why that was so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: No, they didn't. They just never brought anything home, they would just come bare armed, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: And when your sons were at home, and this son when he was at home, did they take any part in the patrolling of the Territorial Defence Forces in the area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: Yes, they would go out overnight there. They would patrol the village, walk around the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Did they have any scheduled duty from the Territorial Defence, the actual scheduled hours when they were supposed to patrol the village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: I presume they did, because they had to go out, and as they did go out, I presume that they did, but they didn't have any armaments.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: But did anyone give them any weapons for the patrol duty?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: I don't know that. No one brought any weapons to the house, and I'm not sure whether somebody gave them any weapons out there, outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: But do you know what the patrolling was like?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: No, I have no idea. They would leave at night, and we ourselves never left the house at night.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: That's as far as the sons are concerned. What about your husband, was he involved in Territorial Defence activities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Did he have any weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: What was he doing in the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: Well, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Did he have any duty?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: No, I really don't know. I just know that they went with (redacted), and they would walk around.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Now, your husband who was just with the Territorial Defence force, did he have any uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: No, no. He only had his civilian clothes which he wore.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: When he patrolled he would also wear civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: And your sons, when they came from the front-line, when they went patrolling did they do so in uniforms or civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: It depended. Sometimes in civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: It was not a definite apparel?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: No, no. Sometimes they would just wear whatever they had on, and sometimes they would put on civilian clothes because the uniforms had to be washed and they had to return to the frontlines in a couple of days, and it would only take a short while.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Now, that part is over. Can I ask you; when you fled, they put you up in Croatian houses, in two Croatian houses, rather?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, did you know what had happened to the Croats who were the owners of those houses? Were they --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: No, we didn't know. I don't know anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: But they must have been exiled. You came to empty houses.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: I don't know. We came there, we didn't see anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: But what had happened to those people? Had they fled or where were the owners of those houses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: I don't know. I have no idea. I had no way of knowing. We didn't see anyone there. They had left, I think. We didn't see anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Did you talk to the owners of those houses? But various stories were bandied around the village, so the Muslims must have talked among themselves what had happened to the owners of those husbands. Did you talk to the Muslims what had happened to them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: I was not interested in all of that. I had my own problems. I had had surgery. I had a fresh wound, a sutured wound, and I had just been discharged from the hospital. I really didn't care. I didn't see anyone. I only know that I kept walking and fleeing.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: I appreciate all of that. Yeah, I know, but I would like to know what happened to the owners of those Croatian houses. Were they also walking on and fleeing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: Probably, yes, they were, of course. All of us were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to interpose an objection at this point, that these questions have now been asked multiple times and the answer has always been she doesn't know, and we would request that perhaps Defence attorney, Mr. Radovic, might move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. Counsel Radovic, I wonder whether you could kindly move on to another question. It is true that you have already put this question many times. Sorry, there's no translation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We didn't hear any translation into English.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: There was a translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: I shall repeat. I shall repeat what I've just said. I've just said that the witness was just about to answer the question, and she started her story when Mr. Moskowitz interrupted, but never mind, I shall continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: No. I had the feeling that the witness said that she did not know, and she was not interested in knowing where the Croatian owners of those houses were. I see -- of course, I do appreciate the relevance of your point, but I think the witness has already answered that she was not in a position to answer. She did not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that I have gathered more or less what it is about, so I shall not pursue this line of questioning anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you ended up in a village which was predominantly populated by Serbs.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Will you now tell me what happened to the Serb owner of that house and what had happened to the Serbs of that village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: The Serbs from that village had gone, and who was in the houses, I really don't know. Whether it was only the army or old people, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know why they had left? Did they go at the moment when the B and H army had taken the village or at some other time, or do you not know at all why they had left, which is not all that important?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: They had gone. That's all I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now let us go back to the 16th of April, the day the attack started, where there were various statements for various witnesses. You said that it was raining. Are you certain that it was raining?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: Yes, I am certain it was raining. How would I not be certain? It was raining. And I had nothing on me; I was wearing nothing. I had just what I was wearing when we got up in the morning. We went out and we were barefoot and had no overcoats or anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Was it raining heavily? Were you wet when you went up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: No. There was a drizzle. We did get up to the hill wet and hungry, but we dried off.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Can we say that there was just a drizzle, no heavy rainfall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: That's right, there was a drizzle, light rain. I know that I was very muddy and that my children were muddy and my daughter, and we sat around in the house where they took us in from Friday to Sunday.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm not interested in what happened later on, I'm just interested in that time. Very well. Thank you. Can you describe the uniforms that the soldiers, you had seen the day before the attack, were wearing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: Well, the uniforms were the kind of multi-coloured or HVO camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: You said that they were patterned. Is it what we call a camouflage uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: Well, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: The pattern, different colours.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. President, I have no further questions to ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Counsel Radovic. Counsel Slokovic-Glumac?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have no questions of the witness. My colleague has exhausted them all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Moskowitz, would you like to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: We have no re-examination questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I have one question which is a follow-up to what Counsel Radovic asked you. Witness M, you said that at one point, at some stage after the 16th of April, you went to a village, and I can't remember the name of that village, but where you were put up in a Croatian house. My question is as follows: Were there any Croats in that village when you went there and were given --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Who was then --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: No, there was nobody. There were no Croats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Only Muslims?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: Only Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I think there is probably no objection to the witness being released. Witness M, thank you so much for coming here to give evidence in court. You may now be released.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M.
utterances.text: Thank you too. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: So we move on to the former Witness 4, which is now Witness 2?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Mr. President, this may be a good time to finish the unfinished business of Friday in which I think Defence counsel were going to make a presentation. I say this may be a good time because we are, I think, bringing some witnesses over, and we're not exactly sure they're precisely here yet, but we know that they are coming, so this may be a good time for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. I turn to Counsel Pavkovic to ask whether the Defence counsel are prepared to set out their views on the issue discussed on Friday, actually raised by the Defence; namely, the question of contacts between the Prosecution and their witnesses and, in future, the Defence and their witnesses. Have you reached a joint position so that one of you can speak on behalf of everybody?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we have, Your Honours. I think that my colleague, Mr. Moskowitz, has made good use of the time. I will be fairly brief in presenting the stand of the Defence. It is a united stand, and I speak on behalf of all my colleagues. The Defence counsel reviewed the numerous aspects of this particular issue and have weighed many reasons, both for and against the motion that they put forward. They started out in their conclusions from the following premise: First of all, we are very grateful to the Trial Chamber for assessing this issue as an important one in the light that it was presented and for enabling us to present our views. The Defence, first of all, assess that it is acceptable, that the thesis put forward by the Prosecutor is acceptable in the portion which he presented on Friday, the 18th of September, that the witness, having appeared before the Trial Chamber, is a court witness from that time on, regardless of the party that brought him to the courtroom and that he is duty-bound to speak the truth according to the oath that he has taken. However, the Defence take note of the following fact, and this came from amongst our ranks, that the question of prohibiting contacts with witnesses should be made when the Prosecutor has already listened to a considerable number of witnesses called by him, particularly the important ones, and in the proceedings so far, in the proceedings that have taken place, that he could have had an advantage. In this connection, the Defence would like to express our concern that this could lead to a imbalance in the parties, an unequal position for the two parties, if we were to accept another regime, another system, and thereby upset the right of the accused to a just and fair trial. The Defence further takes note that in this Trial Chamber, we have witnesses called with specific characteristics; that is to say, they are also the victims of the events that took place or they are individuals who have suffered personal losses, so that witnesses of this kind are very sensitive in the areas they are questioned on and so their statements too could wield influence. Therefore, it would be a good idea if we were to bear in mind the fact that in these contacts, we have, in fact, before us situations where we encourage the witness to recall the events of the past when suggestions are made to him to recall the situation and the events. Before I present our views, our final views, I would like to say that Defence counsel bore in mind the legal understanding presented by Judge Mumba on Friday, and bearing in mind the Furundzija case and the initiative taken by the Defence counsel in that case to prohibit contact. On the basis of these views and situations, Defence counsel feel as follows: They feel that from the moment when the witness is brought before the Trial Chamber and makes the formal declaration that he will speak the truth when he takes the oath, from that moment on, he becomes a court witness. Therefore, there can be no further contacts with the witness by anybody, regardless of who brought the witness to the courtroom, whether it was the Prosecution or the Defence, without, of course, a decision by the Trial Chamber. If this were to be the subject of discussion, Defence counsel consider that we should bear in mind an exception from this general view, and that is that at the proposal of the parties concerned, or the witness himself, and having received authorisation by the Trial Chamber and under its supervision, in special cases contacts could be allowed, in extraordinary cases. Defence counsel would like to remind the Trial Chamber that this view, presented by them, does not have any basis in rules of proceedings but that it can be in keeping with the spirit of the Statute and general legal proceedings which ensure that during a hearing we get as close to the truth and see the truth as it stands. Finally, we should like to request that the Trial Chamber bear in mind what we have just said and that it should consider all the different aspects of this issue and give a ruling in the matter. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I wonder whether the Prosecution would like to comment? No. Not necessary. Yes, your position was very clear. All right. Well, I would like to thank Counsel Pavkovic and all the other counsel for their position. Now it is very clear to us what the position of both the Defence and the Prosecution is, and we will rule on this matter probably by tomorrow morning. I suggest that we now should break and we will reconvene at quarter past eleven sharp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: (The witness entered court).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: First of all, I will ask the witness to read out the solemn declaration. Could you please stand and read out the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Witness, would you care to give out your full identity and say when you were born and who you are?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL SEAN DOOLEY.
utterances.text: Certainly. I am Major Michael Dooley and I was born on the 15th of March, 1966.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could you state to the Tribunal what your present assignment is?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL SEAN DOOLEY.
utterances.text: I am the operations officer of One Brigade which forms a part of the Allied Rapid Reaction Corps in the NATO headquarters, joint headquarters in Rheindahlen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could you state what your professional background and experience is and what your training was?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL SEAN DOOLEY.
utterances.text: Certainly. I joined the army in 1990 and joined the Royal Corps Signals. In 1992, I was assigned as a platoon commander to the First Battalion, the Cheshire regiment, for a tour of about 18 months, and there I was a Warrior platoon commander. After that, I went to Catterick, where I was an infantry advisor to the Royal Signals, and my next assignment was to 20 Armoured Brigade as an operations officer. I was then sent to the Royal Military Academy Sandhurst, where I was an instructor there, and then recently, I have been posted to my current assignment, which is the operations officer within One Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: When were you assigned or were you sent to Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL SEAN DOOLEY.
utterances.text: I was posted, what we call Operation Grapple 1, which was in October 1992, and we left in May 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: What was your mission? What were you supposed to do in Bosnia during that time?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL SEAN DOOLEY.
utterances.text: Our initial mission was to protect UNHCR convoys providing humanitarian aid to victims of the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You were a platoon commander in Bosnia, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL SEAN DOOLEY.
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could you tell us how a platoon is made up? What is the composition of a platoon?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL SEAN DOOLEY.
utterances.text: Certainly. There were approximately 36 soldiers in the platoon, and the platoon had four armoured vehicles called Warriors under command.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I would like us to turn to the period preceding April 1993. You were then an observer in that area. Could you tell us what you witnessed as to the forces present in the area of Vitez? Did you see forces from the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina? Did you see HVO forces? Could you tell this to the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL SEAN DOOLEY.
utterances.text: Certainly. Could I just clarify one point? Do you want me to go from the start of the tour, from October, or immediately preceding April?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Well, a period that stretches from October '92 up to April 1993.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL SEAN DOOLEY.
utterances.text: Certainly. Initially, the area was divided into a number of localised groups of mainly Croatian and BiH troops. The general concentrations were: Travnik was strongly BiH, Vitez was mostly Croatian, although there were BiH there, and then it was a mixture as you went through the Lasva Valley between Croatian and BiH troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: What did you think of the condition in which the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina was at that time? How was it armed? What was its equipment?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL SEAN DOOLEY.
utterances.text: Certainly. They were weak in most areas with the exception of Travnik where they were well-armed with -- when I say "well-armed," they only had automatic weapons. I never saw anything of any reasonable calibre. Certainly in Vitez, all I saw were light automatic weapons and not very many of them. As you went out of Vitez, again small arms only for the ABiH. The Croatians had a number of heavier calibre weapons; for example, they had a .50 calibre automatic anti-aircraft gun mounted on top of a flatbed truck which they used occasionally.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: In the weeks preceding the 16th of April, 1993, let us say during the first two weeks of April 1993, did you notice that there were forces of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina in the region of Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL SEAN DOOLEY.
utterances.text: No, there were no BiH soldiers in the area of Ahmici. There were a few, and not very many -- I mean, hardly any at all -- in Vitez itself. The bulk of the soldiers were over towards Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: In the weeks preceding the 16th of April, 1993, did you sense that the situation was changing in terms of relations between the various communities?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL SEAN DOOLEY.
utterances.text: Yes. There was increased tensions, many instants of shooting in the whole of the valley, really, stretching from Travnik right through Vitez and down towards Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could you tell us how that day of the 16th of April, 1993, was for you, to the best of your recollection? You were on duty, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL SEAN DOOLEY.
utterances.text: Yes, I was. As it happens, I was the operations officer early in the morning, and then at 6.00 in the morning -- I had gone to bed then maybe at 2.00. At 6.00, I was working by one of my platoons and there was large explosions caused by a very large calibre mortar which had been firing on occasion throughout the tour, but those explosions caused me to get out of bed very quickly and move to the operations room. My battalion second-in-command, Major Watters, then told me to go and investigate what was happening in Vitez town itself. I estimate the time I got to Vitez town would be about half past 6.00 maybe, in the morning. Vitez town, there was a lot of smoke from the initial buildings as you enter the town, and there was a lot of firing going on although, because of the echoes with the buildings, it was very difficult to trace where the firing was. So on our initial pass, we went through the centre of the town trying to identify where the firing was coming from. We then radioed in where we thought the firing was coming from, which was the area of the stadium in Vitez, and we went and investigated that area where indeed we saw troops shooting into houses and setting fire to houses using incendiary grenades. Do you want me to carry on through the day?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Well, could you specify which troops you saw on that morning in Vitez and which units did they belong to?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL SEAN DOOLEY.
utterances.text: I couldn't specify the exact units. I know they were Croatian troops. I recognised their uniforms, et cetera, and they were -- when I saw them, they were only shooting at civilians, and there were no BiH troops in Vitez. There were no BiH casualties in uniform, they were all civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could you carry on that story of the day as it went?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL SEAN DOOLEY.
utterances.text: Certainly. I was then told to go north of Vitez to a village, the name escapes me, because there were threats or there was a chance of shooting going on up there. When I got to that village, everything seemed fine, although the villagers were hiding behind walls, but there was no signs of fighting that I could see. Meanwhile, the fighting was continuing in Vitez town, so we went back to Vitez. It is important to note that whenever we arrived in an area of Vitez, the fighting in that immediate area would stop. The troops, Croatian troops, would go to ground, would just wait until such a point as we left. And normally, when we went to ground or we stopped, the fighting would happen somewhere else in the town and we would hear that, so we would go elsewhere and it would start, maybe the area we just left. At some point around lunch time, it came over my radio to go to the village of Ahmici where there was reported instants of fighting there. So I drove to Ahmici from Vitez with the four Warriors and drove down the main road -- maybe I can show you. Here (indicating). And I drove up to the car park, which is just north of the cemetery here, and then drove back again, and all I was doing at this point was seeing what was going on in this area here (indicating), only from the road. I then radioed in to my officer commanding, Major Martin Thomas, what was happening. I said there was a lot of dead people on the sides of the road near the houses, and as far as I could see, although there was the occasional shot coming down from the south-west, there was no resistance and nobody alive that I could see. There were some locals in this area here (indicating) who wanted to get to their dead, so I told my officer commanding this. He said to wait until he sent some reinforcements, which was a light cavalry troop of four scimitars and an armoured ambulance, and so I waited for them to the south-east here in a car park until the reinforcements arrived from Vitez camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: So this was your first visit to Ahmici, wasn't it? What time was it when you first got to Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL SEAN DOOLEY.
utterances.text: It was approximately noon.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: So you were leading four armoured vehicles; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL SEAN DOOLEY.
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You yourself, which vehicle were you in?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL SEAN DOOLEY.
utterances.text: I would always be in the forward most vehicle. The composition of the platoon, the four armoured vehicles, were such that there would always be me in the lead, followed by one of my corporals in a second Warrior, followed by my platoon sergeants -- this is slightly confusing. I have two platoon sergeants: one is a Warrior platoon sergeant, he commands an armoured vehicle, he would be in the third vehicle, and then his corporal would be in the fourth vehicle, and that was always the format that we used.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: During this first visit to Ahmici, did you notice that there was firing?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL SEAN DOOLEY.
utterances.text: Yes. On the initial visit, though, it wasn't great, but there was sufficient that we were unwilling to go investigating random shooting. But it wasn't a great deal of firing, it was just the occasional shot.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: So it is during this initial visit that a video film was taken by one of your men; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL SEAN DOOLEY.
utterances.text: That is correct. It was on the initial pass, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, is it possible to see this video clip? You are aware of it already because it was seen during the testimony of Witness G, but since Major Dooley is here with us, I would like him to make comment, if any. This is Exhibit 120. Can we see this? (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Major Dooley, please go ahead with your comments, if you have any, when you wish to do so.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL SEAN DOOLEY.
utterances.text: Certainly. This is obviously the view from the road, and this is very much what we saw in the initial pass. As you can see, as far as we were aware, there was nobody alive at this point. There were a number of dead bodies, perhaps more than is shown on this video. We could see them through the doors and beside the housing, and all it seemed to us at this point was that it was a clean-up operation. There was occasional firing from the high ground behind you there, and perhaps -- it doesn't show so well in the video here, but there was a lot of smoke which obscured the view to the extreme north-west. In this particular scene, the very front vehicle that you just saw was where I was, and this would be my platoon sergeant who is videoing at the moment. I never saw anybody alive. My platoon sergeant obviously caught this on camera, but I never actually saw anybody; otherwise, that would have influenced, perhaps, a few things I did later. This is later on the clean-up operation which would have probably been past number 2, and the reason I say that is we're not under fire here, which happens later on, and I would estimate that in this particular scene, I would be behind the building that's on the left-hand side of the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Speaking of your second pass in Ahmici from the main road, do you remember whether there was a lot of firing?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL SEAN DOOLEY.
utterances.text: Yes. Each pass that happened, it became increasingly more violent. The first pass, not a great deal happened. We saw that from the video. The second pass -- I estimate this is probably the second pass because we're not under a great deal of fire here. We took -- I can show on the map. We took the dead, which I would probably estimate around six in number because that's all we could get in the ambulance, from this area here (indicating), which I think is what they're showing on the map -- on the video, to the car park here where we had seen some Muslims earlier trying to get to their dead, and line them up on the car park so that they could get to their dead. And then we drove -- once we had done that, we drove back again to this area for a third time. Do you want to carry on?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL SEAN DOOLEY.
utterances.text: On the third pass, we came back again with more bodies from roughly the same area, but the shooting was beginning to increase, and we had to form a wall using the Warriors lined up end to end, so that any bullets that were coming from this area here, firing down this way (indicating), wouldn't hit us. We formed a horizontal wall, I would say, using the Warriors, all facing up the hill, and then brought the ambulance in behind, and then we all moved the bodies into the ambulance, so that the armoured vehicle was between us and any shooting. Although it looks very clear here, the smoke was such that we couldn't see where the shooting was coming from. All we could tell was it was a very large calibre, I estimate about .50, and we can tell that by the size of the tracer round that was going through the smoke towards us. We couldn't engage it -- we would have engaged it if we had been fired at -- we couldn't engage it because we couldn't identify the target because of the smoke. On the third pass, we came back here, unloaded the bodies, but there was beginning to be firing down here. There hadn't been firing down here before on our earlier passes. It was beginning to, but we lined up maybe another five to six casualties there, making somewhere between ten and twelve. I forget how many. But there was no sign of anybody around here at that point. The people who were waiting for the casualties before had gone. On our fourth pass, we came back to here -- again, at this point, I had seen nobody alive. I hadn't seen what the platoon sergeant had seen on the video. On the fourth pass, the firing was becoming very intense and the soldiers were getting fired into the buildings near where they were evacuating dead people. So as far as I could see, there was no point in staying there and maybe getting one of my soldiers wounded because there was nobody alive to protect, so what was the point picking up casualties? You can do that any time. There was certainly nobody even wounded. They were all dead as far as I could see. We then took those people back to this area here (indicating), and we came under fire at this point from two directions, from this direction and from this direction (indicating), and it was sufficiently great for me not to unload any casualties there, to keep everybody inside the Warriors, because, again, my soldiers would become injured for no reason. It was at this point that I made the decision to move those dead people back to Vitez town where I was told that there was a medical centre, and so I took them to the town itself. As it happens, I took them to a Croatian medical centre -- I didn't realise it was Croatian at the time -- I took them there, and we unloaded the dead people in a morgue that was beside a makeshift operating theatre.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could one say that between the first and the fourth pass, the situation had worsened in Ahmici due to the firing that was more intense, more heavy firing then?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL SEAN DOOLEY.
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes, that's exactly what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You also stated that on your third pass, you had seen heavy calibre firing coming from inside the village. Could you specify, be more precise, as to the areas from where the firing came?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL SEAN DOOLEY.
utterances.text: Within Ahmici itself on that day, there was only one area firing ever came from, although we could not see it, we knew the direction, and it was approximately here (indicating), and as I say, it was about .50 calibre. You could tell by the sound that the weapon made and the size of the tracer round coming through the smoke. Sorry. There's one other piece I missed as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could you tell us approximately what time it was when you noticed this big calibre?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me interrupt to clarify something. The witness has said that the firing came from a particular point, and that point was referred to earlier, in earlier evidence, as the turning circle, and I think the record should make that clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Absolutely, Judge. Also it is good to specify this for the transcript. Let us say that the witness stated as the area from where the heavy calibre firing was coming, which he noticed on his third passage, that he indicated the area close to the parking area designated as Grabovi Sutre where the houses of some of the accused, of the Kupreskic accused, are to be found.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could you tell us what time it was when you noted this firing coming from the Sutre area?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL SEAN DOOLEY.
utterances.text: It's probably important to note that on all of the passing, there was shooting, but the specific heavy firing would have been maybe 13.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: When did you carry out your last visit to Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL SEAN DOOLEY.
utterances.text: It's difficult to say, obviously, but I would say maybe 15.00, 15.30, because I had one more trip to do, and I remember getting back to the camp when it was dark, so ... When I say "one more trip," not to Ahmici, to the village north of Vitez. There was one important thing that I forgot to mention on my first run, and that was that we witnessed, in this ravine here (indicating), maybe ten -- I couldn't see beyond that because there was smoke -- maybe ten Croatian soldiers lying here facing this way. It seemed to me that that was a cut-off group. It was difficult to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: How were the soldiers dressed that you saw in that ditch?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL SEAN DOOLEY.
utterances.text: They were in the standard Croatian, American-style camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: For you, is there no doubt as their belonging to the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL SEAN DOOLEY.
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could you once again show us on the map where those soldiers were?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL SEAN DOOLEY.
utterances.text: There's a very definite ravine here, and they were lying on this side of the bank and below the bank and looking this way. They tried to hide as we went past in our Warriors, but because of the height of the Warrior we could see them down in the ravine.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: For the sake of the transcript, we should state that this ravine or this ditch is parallel to the road leading to the Ahmici village, towards Vitez. This ravine is very visible on the map, on the aerial photograph. Mr. Witness, could you tell us how many bodies you were able to collect in Ahmici, numbers of bodies you found and collected on that day in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL SEAN DOOLEY.
utterances.text: Less than 20 we collected on the three passes. I maybe put -- I had seen 10 or 12 in this car park, and then maybe 6, maybe a few more in the morgue. And the number of bodies seen we could have gone all day, but had I seen anybody alive, that would have changed my whole perception, but because they were -- all looked dead, there was no point in staying.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: In which area did you find all these bodies?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL SEAN DOOLEY.
utterances.text: They were from approximately here through to approximately here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Were they male, female bodies, bodies of old people, of children?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL SEAN DOOLEY.
utterances.text: The ones that we collected were male and female. All of them were in their civilian clothes. Most of whom weren't wearing shoes, because that was pointed out by one of my soldiers, which suggested that is they were surprised. I saw no children killed, but there were certainly male and female, and quite a few older people.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Did you see any weapons close to those bodies?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL SEAN DOOLEY.
utterances.text: They were all civilians. And perhaps an important point to note here was that the number of bullet wounds in each of the victims was great, which would suggest to me that the shooting was from a very close proximity. Obviously the greater the proximity, the wider the spread, the less the bullet numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Which means that automatic guns were used at close range; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL SEAN DOOLEY.
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd like another video clip, a short video clip, to be displayed. It is a video clip coming from the Croatian television, from the Croatian community of ethnic Bosna, coming from the Zenica studio. I'd like the witness to make comments. (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: It's important to have the soundtrack. Is it possible to have the soundtrack? Because you can hear the shooting or the firing, and I'd like the witness to be able to identify the weapons used. Can we have it from the very beginning again? A man will be seen who's giving a comment. I have the English transcript of this commentary which was originally in Croatian. I'd like to hand this over.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The video will be marked 179 and the transcript 179-A.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I'm very sorry, Mr. President, but I think it's important to have the soundtrack of that video clip. (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I wonder whether we could ask the technicians to make sure that we can hear the sound. We need some time, so it seems. Could you move on to other questions, then we will be able to have the video clip and the soundtrack towards the end?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, could you state your view of what happened to Ahmici, say to the Tribunal what you think happened on that day? What do you think happened that day in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL SEAN DOOLEY.
utterances.text: Obviously I know the early morning events through talking to friends from the same battalion who had been there earlier than I was, but it appears, certainly when I got there at 12.00, the initial attack had been -- was over. The people I picked up were all trying to go towards the road. They were all at the front of the houses and going this way, which again would coincide with the fire that we saw later coming from this point here, that they seemed to be fleeing in this direction. A lot of the bodies around here had a number of wounds coming in through their right-hand side as well as the front, which again would tie up to the fact that they were hit by cross-fire from this direction -- sorry, this direction, and indeed, from the front of them, because they were hit from this point. So where they were actually shot was different to the weapon that was up here, and indeed the calibre of weapon used was a much smaller, which suggests small-arms fire from the front and side. Certainly when I got there it looked like they'd all been killed from that point. I think later in the day, as we were gathering up the dead, they decided that they didn't want us there any more, which is why they were firing upon us at that point, firing through the smoke at where they thought we were. Bear in mind we couldn't see them, and we had at times magnification sights on the Warriors, so they probably wouldn't be able to see us specifically, they'd just know by the noise of the vehicles roughly where we were. And I think that's probably why they train the fire on us in our area. Really, that's all I could say. It seemed to me that they pushed them down from here and were waiting for them on the road and from this direction here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Do you think this was a military operation? Would you qualify this as being a military operation, meaning carried out by the Croats?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL SEAN DOOLEY.
utterances.text: I didn't see evidence of Croat soldiers that would help me make that impression, but also it was a very well-coordinated attack. The whole day was very cleverly coordinated. Wherever we were with our Warriors the fighting would die down, and so they clearly had radio communications they started somewhere else, and so we were constantly chasing round. So it was very clear to me the whole operation was conducted by the military, and with cut-off groups here, firing points on the hard standing up there. It seemed reasonably well put together by somebody who had a good grasp of tactics.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: With your leave, Mr. President, I would like to ask the view of the witness on a statement made by Mr. Hayman in another case presently being heard before another trial Chamber in the Blaskic case. This is a public document. The initial statements by -- opening statement by Mr. Hayman -- let me, please, finish before -- allow me to conclude my sentence. Yes. This is the only statement by Mr. Hayman on behalf of Mr. Blaskic, who, at a given point in time, supplied information as to what, in his view, happened on the 16th of April, 1993 in Ahmici. This is a public document, the statement was made publicly, and I'd like to submit this to the witness, to show him the contents of this opening statement regarding Ahmici. This is half a page long, so as to have his comment. Thank you, I've finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Counsel Radovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we object to the use and presentation in this particular case of statements made by witnesses in another case, actually, the statements of Defence counsel appearing on behalf of another client in another case. I believe that is totally irrelevant. The more so as none of the accused in the Blaskic case could have had any influence whatsoever on the statement in question. So I believe that that statement is not involved and of relevance in this particular case, that we are here on today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Terrier, could you possibly sum up in a few words what the opening statement is, so as to give us the gist of it? I believe this opening statement was delivered by Mr. Hayman, and if I understood it properly, this reflects the position adopted by General Blaskic, but you could, perhaps, sum up in a few words the gist of the statement and then ask a question. I suppose you're going to ask this witness what he thinks of it as a military expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Yes, as a military expert but also as a factual witness as he was in Ahmici on the 16th of April, 1993 towards noon and towards 3.30, approximately, in the afternoon. This statement was made by Mr. Hayman on the 7th of September in another case before another Trial Chamber of this Tribunal, and I suppose his opinion reflects that of General Blaskic, but I believe this is -- I take it a statement by Mr. Hayman. This is what he says -- so I'm giving you the basic meaning of it, but I do have the full statement for you, Judges, and for the Defence counsel, the entire statement made by Mr. Hayman. He said that there was, indeed, the massacre of Muslim civilians in Ahmici; that all the Muslim houses were burned down in Ahmici; that, however, according to Mr. Hayman, this massacre is to be seen within the framework of a military operation, because there was organised resistance and major organised resistance in Ahmici on the 16th of April, 1993. Here is my first question to the witness: Did you notice that on the 16th of April, 1993, in Ahmici, there was a major organised resistance in the face of an attack launch on the village?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL SEAN DOOLEY.
utterances.text: There was absolutely no resistance whatsoever, and there were no signs at all of ABiH troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: The second question: Mr. Hayman stated that this massacre was completed around noon or towards the end of the late morning on the 16th of April, 1993. Is this what you also think?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL SEAN DOOLEY.
utterances.text: That would be my opinion, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I think that we're now in a position to see the short video clip. (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: (Interpreting commentary from video tape) ... "We are two kilometres away from Vitez, but we shall probably not be able to go on. We have mines in the area and you can see for yourself that the fighting is going on here."

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Yes, I would like to ask a few questions following this video clip. What we have just seen on this clip, does that match your recollection of Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL SEAN DOOLEY.
utterances.text: Yes. You can see from the video that there was heavy smoke which obscured our view of the hill, which is probably where he was filming from, but at a lower level we couldn't see it. And also, you could hear the high-calibre weapon which was making the pronounced cracks. A small-arms weapon wouldn't make that noise.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: The heavy-calibre weapons, could you specify the type of weapons at all?
